stem: Sluysmans and Colan proposed that the optimal size of a cardiovascular structure minimizes the hemodynamic cost of providing blood flow. According to this **principle of minimal work**, the optimal radius of a valve or vessel is the radius that:

choices.text: Minimizes viscous energy loss alone, which falls as the radius increases
Minimizes the inertial energy content of blood alone
Minimizes the sum of viscous energy loss and inertial energy content
Is calculated for the resting cardiac output only
Stays the same whatever the cardiac output

explanation.text: The optimal radius sits at the **minimum of the total energy loss curve**: the sum of **viscous energy loss** and **inertial energy content**.

explanation.title: Two energies pull in opposite directions

branches.label: viscous
branches.text: Shear stress is related to **inverse** radius -> larger radius, less viscous loss

branches.label: inertial
branches.text: Inertial energy (pulsatile flow) is **directly** related to radius

explanation.caption: Fig. 1.32: optimal aortic valve radius, normal subject with BSA 1 m²
head: Theoretical cardiac output
Represents
Optimal radius

explanation.text: These two values are the **theoretical range of normal** optimal aortic valve radius for this BSA: normal pathways carry flow at rest **and** during exercise and stress with little or no pressure drop.
To achieve minimum work requires minimizing viscous energy (shear stress related to inverse vessel radius) and inertial energy related to pulsatile flow, which is directly related to radius

choiceNotes.a: Viscous loss alone keeps falling as the radius grows; the optimum is where the **total** of viscous and inertial energy is lowest.
choiceNotes.b: Inertial energy rises with radius; minimizing it alone ignores viscous loss. The optimum balances **both**.
choiceNotes.d: Fig. 1.32 gives an optimum at rest (0.45 cm) **and** at maximal exercise (0.8 cm); together they form the theoretical normal range.
choiceNotes.e: In Fig. 1.32 the optimal radius is larger at the higher cardiac output (0.8 cm vs 0.45 cm).

source.loc: p. 23, Dimensions of Normal Cardiac and Great Artery Pathways; Fig. 1.32

stem: A team wants to compare the size of the aorta in a neonate with that in an adult. According to the energy optimization relationship described by Sluysmans and Colan, the normal **diameter** of a blood vessel is related to body surface area (BSA) as:

choices.text: BSA^0.5^ (the square root of BSA)
BSA^1^ (a linear relationship)
BSA^2^ (the square of BSA)
BSA^1.5^ (BSA to the power 1.5)
Independent of BSA (a constant)

explanation.text: **Diameter** scales with the **square root of BSA** (BSA^0.5^); **area** scales **linearly** with BSA.

explanation.caption: How normal size relates to BSA
head: Measured quantity
Relationship to BSA

explanation.text: Sluysmans and Colan showed that this **optimization of energy is related to BSA** over a wide range of sizes of mammals, including humans.

explanation.title: Area vs diameter
explanation.text: Dividing a dimension by BSA ("per square meter BSA") presumes a strictly linear relation. That fits an **area**, not a **diameter**.
For the valve and blood vessel area, this relationship is linear with BSA; for the diameter of vessels, this relationship is the square root of BSA (BSA^0.5^).

choiceNotes.b: A linear relationship with BSA applies to valve and vessel **area**, not diameter.
choiceNotes.c: The source gives a square-root (BSA^0.5^) relationship for diameter, not BSA squared.
choiceNotes.d: The source gives an exponent of 0.5 for diameter, not 1.5.
choiceNotes.e: The optimization of energy is related to BSA over a wide range of sizes of mammals, so diameter is not independent of BSA.

source.loc: p. 23, Dimensions of Normal Cardiac and Great Artery Pathways

stem: A congenital heart program reports aortic valve **diameters** "per square meter BSA" (diameter divided by BSA) to compare patients ranging from neonates to adults. What is the main problem with this approach?

choices.text: Indexing should be done to height, never to BSA
A valve diameter cannot be measured by echocardiography
BSA indexing is valid only for prosthesis–patient mismatch
It assumes diameter varies linearly with BSA
Dividing by BSA turns the value into a z score

explanation.text: Expressing a dimension "per square meter BSA" **presumes a strictly linear relation** with BSA. That is probably accurate for an **area** but **inaccurate for a diameter**.
What must be achieved is normalization that is ==constant across body size from smallest neonate to adult==.

explanation.title: Plain centimeters
explanation.text: Some who work only with adults express aortic size simply in centimeters. This is **unacceptable** when the population ranges from very young to very old.
If a structure’s area is measured, the relationship to BSA is probably accurate. If instead a diameter of a structure is normalized this way, it will be inaccurate.

choiceNotes.a: Height is one option (for example for thoracic aorta diameter), but the source says the preference is generally for normalizing to **BSA**.
choiceNotes.b: Echocardiography is the most used modality for measuring pathway dimensions.
choiceNotes.c: Prosthesis–patient mismatch is one example of BSA normalization; the general preference is for BSA, not only for that use.
choiceNotes.e: A z score is the number of standard deviations from the mean normal value for BSA, not a value divided by BSA.

stem: Before surgery, a surgeon judges "by eye" on an image that a child's pathway is too small for a good repair, without measuring it. Which error specific to such **subjective** size evaluation does the source describe?

choices.text: Failure to correct the image for magnification
Unconscious comparison with a neighboring unusually large structure
Assuming an elliptical instead of a circular cross-section
Measuring in a different phase of the cardiac cycle
Using normal values from a different imaging modality

explanation.text: Subjective size evaluation may be **grossly inaccurate** because the structure is unconsciously compared with a **neighboring unusually large structure**.

children: with a neighboring unusually large structure

steps.text: Some pathways are **so small** they preclude a satisfactory outcome
Prediction of outcome from dimensions becomes important

steps.label: therefore
steps.text: ==Measurements== and their relation to outcome are required for reproducible, accurate predictions

explanation.text: this evaluation may be grossly inaccurate because of unconscious comparison of the size of the structure in question with that of a neighboring unusually large structure.

choiceNotes.a: Magnification correction applies to dimensions **measured** by cineangiography, not to a judgment by eye.
choiceNotes.c: Choosing a circular or elliptical shape is part of **measuring** a dimension and calculating area.
choiceNotes.d: Phase of the cardiac cycle is a factor that must be controlled when **measuring** and interpreting dimensions.
choiceNotes.e: Relating a measurement to normal values from another modality concerns **measured** dimensions; it is not the error of subjective evaluation.

source.loc: p. 23, Dimensions of Normal Cardiac and Great Artery Pathways

stem: On 2D imaging, a valve orifice is clearly **oval** rather than round. Which approach to its cross-sectional area does the source describe for this situation?

choices.text: Measure one diameter and assume a circular shape
Measure its circumference in a fixed autopsy specimen
Index the single diameter to body surface area
Average the diameters measured in systole and diastole
Measure major and minor axes; use an ellipse equation

explanation.text: For an elliptical shape, the **major and minor axes** are measured and area is calculated with an **equation that applies to ellipses**.
These factors **must be specifically controlled** in making and interpreting the measurements.
In other circumstances, an elliptical shape is assumed, major and minor axes are measured, and area is calculated with an equation that applies to ellipses.

choiceNotes.a: A single diameter with an assumed **circular** shape is the approach for round structures, not for an elliptical one.
choiceNotes.b: Autopsy measurement is a different source of dimensions; the stem concerns an orifice seen on imaging.
choiceNotes.c: Indexing is normalization to body size; it does not give the cross-sectional area.
choiceNotes.d: Phase of the cardiac cycle is a factor to control when interpreting measurements; it is not the method for an elliptical area.

stem: A child with a borderline-small valve needs its dimension followed over several years before a surgical decision. Which reason does the source give for echocardiography having become the **most used** modality for measuring pathway dimensions?

choices.text: Dimensions can be followed serially without radiation or sedation
It is the only modality for which normal values exist
Its dimensions match autopsy dimensions exactly at every size
It always measures cross-sectional area directly
Its values need no relation to body size

explanation.text: Echocardiography is the most used modality partly because dimensions can be **followed serially without radiation or sedation**.

items: Dimensions have been measured in **autopsy specimens**, by **cineangiography** (must be corrected for **magnification**), by **echocardiography** (M-mode, 2D, 3D), and increasingly by **MRI** and **CT**.
By echocardiography, dimensions have been determined at nearly all ages, **from fetal to age 90 years**.
The **Pediatric Heart Network** study (3215 healthy children, 0 to 18 years) is the largest source of data, with allometric equations in its supplement.

explanation.title: No normal values for your modality?
explanation.text: Normal values are generally **not available in each modality**, so dimensions must be related to available normal values, ==even if from a different modality==.
Echocardiography has evolved as the most used modality for measuring these dimensions, in part because the dimensions can be easily followed serially without radiation or sedation.

choiceNotes.b: Normal dimensions also come from autopsy specimens (for example Table 1.1); normal values are generally not available in **each** modality.
choiceNotes.c: Echocardiographic and autopsy dimensions differ; for the mitral valve, echo values were about 33% larger below about 0.5 m² BSA.
choiceNotes.d: Cross-sectional area can be measured directly only under some circumstances, such as by **3D** echocardiography, CT or MRI.
choiceNotes.e: Measured dimensions generally must be related to normal dimensions, which vary with body size and age.

source.loc: p. 25, Use of Standardized Cardiac Dimensions in Surgical Decisions; Table 1.1

stem: A 78-year-old woman's echocardiogram before surgery shows a **more acute septoaortic angle** with a **septal bulge**, without left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. According to the source, this finding is best interpreted as:

choices.text: An early stage of LVOT obstruction
A change seen mainly in children and adolescents
An age-associated change in LVOT geometry
An artifact of 2D echocardiographic measurement
A sign of mild left ventricular dysfunction

explanation.text: Swinne and colleagues described **age-associated changes in LVOT geometry** in normal subjects, mostly **after age 70**; they may be **degenerative changes of aging**.

children: may be degenerative changes of aging

explanation.text: A septal bulge in an elderly patient is **not by itself** LVOT obstruction: in these normal subjects it was not associated with obstruction.

These changes consist of a more acute septoaortic angle or septal bulge that is not associated with left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. These may represent degenerative changes associated with aging.

choiceNotes.a: The source says this septal bulge is **not associated** with LVOT obstruction.
choiceNotes.b: These changes were observed in normal subjects **mostly after age 70**.
choiceNotes.d: They are described as real age-associated changes in LVOT geometry observed in normal subjects.
choiceNotes.e: Mild left ventricular dysfunction is the finding the source describes in **preterm infants**, not these aging changes.

stem: To follow a patient's aortic size, a team expresses the aortic diameter relative to the diameter of the **descending aorta at the diaphragm**. This form of normalization is termed:

choices.text: Indexing
A ratio
Standardization
A z score
Allometric growth

explanation.text: Normalization to **another body structure** (such as the descending aorta at the diaphragm) is termed a **ratio**.

explanation.caption: Three kinds of normalization
head: Normalized to
Term
Examples from the source
rows: Height for thoracic aorta diameter; BSA for prosthesis–patient mismatch
z score (standard deviations from the normal mean)

explanation.text: The preference is generally for normalizing to **BSA**.
Normalization may also be to another structure, such as the size of the descending aorta at the diaphragm. Normalization to another body structure generally is termed a ratio.

choiceNotes.a: Indexing is normalization to **body size** (for example height, weight or BSA), not to another structure.
choiceNotes.c: Standardization is normalization to **standard normal people**.
choiceNotes.d: A z score is the standardized value: standard deviations from the mean normal value for body size.
choiceNotes.e: Allometric growth is the variation of normal dimensions with body size and age, not a normalization method.

stem: A child's pathway diameter measures 11.0 mm. For normal individuals of the same BSA, regression equations give a mean normal diameter of 14.0 mm with a standard deviation of 1.5 mm (hypothetical values). What is this patient's **z score**?

explanation.text: z = (11.0 − 14.0) / 1.5 = **−2.0**: the valve is two standard deviations **below** the mean normal value for this BSA.

steps.text: **Observed dimension** in the patient of known BSA (11.0 mm)

steps.label: minus
steps.text: **Mean normal dimension** for that BSA (14.0 mm) = −3.0 mm

steps.label: divided by
steps.text: **Standard deviation** of the mean normal dimension (1.5 mm)

explanation.text: The mean and standard deviation refer to **normal individuals of the same BSA as the patient**, obtained from regression analysis and equations. Standardization takes into account that values in normal individuals of the same size **vary**.
Keep the order **observed minus mean**, and divide by the **standard deviation**, not by the mean: a dimension smaller than normal gives a **negative** z.

Once in the normal distribution domain, any given value for a dimension can be expressed in terms of the number of standard deviations of the given value from the mean value of that dimension in normal individuals.

choiceNotes.a: −3.0 mm is only the difference from the mean; it must still be divided by the standard deviation (1.5 mm).
choiceNotes.b: 0.79 is the observed diameter divided by the mean (11.0/14.0); the z score is the difference from the mean divided by the **standard deviation**.
choiceNotes.c: This divides the difference by the mean (14.0 mm); the z score divides by the **standard deviation**.
choiceNotes.e: This multiplies the difference by the standard deviation instead of dividing by it.

stem: A surgeon is given the **z value** of a child's pulmonary valve. As depicted in the chapter (Fig. 1.33), a patient's specific z value corresponds to which quantity?

choices.text: The measured diameter divided by body surface area
The observed diameter as a percentage of the mean normal
The percentage by which echo exceeds autopsy size
The absolute difference in millimeters from normal
The percentile of normals with that size or smaller

explanation.text: A patient with a specific z value has the dimension of the **corresponding percentile of the normal population**: the percentage of normal individuals with **that dimension or a smaller one**.

steps.text: Patient's **z value** on the horizontal axis (−3 to +3)

steps.label: up to the curve
steps.text: S-shaped curve of the normal population

steps.label: across
steps.text: **Percent of population** on the vertical axis = ==percentile==

items: **z = 0**: observed dimension equals the mean normal value for that BSA (middle of the curve).
**Negative z**: smaller than the mean, so a lower percentile.
**Positive z**: larger than the mean, so a higher percentile.

explanation.text: A patient with a specific z value has the dimension of the corresponding percentile of the normal population.
explanation.ref: Chapter 1: Anatomy and Dimensions, p. 24, Fig. 1.33

choiceNotes.a: Dividing by BSA is indexing ("per square meter BSA"), not a z value.
choiceNotes.b: A z value is not a percentage of the mean; a specific z value corresponds to the **percentile of the normal population**.
choiceNotes.c: Echo vs autopsy differences are a comparison of measurement methods; z values make them less important.
choiceNotes.d: The z value expresses the difference in **standard deviations**, not in millimeters, and maps to a percentile of normals.

stem: A center applies a published z-score equation, derived from one population of normal children, to its own patients from a different population. Which **limitation of standardization** does the source emphasize?

choices.text: Normal values and their SD vary between populations
z scores cannot be calculated for neonates or fetuses
z scores can be used only with echocardiographic measurements
z scores magnify differences between echo and autopsy values
The normal distribution domain is mathematically intractable

explanation.text: What is normal, and the **scatter** of normal measurements, **vary from population to population**, particularly the **standard deviation**.

steps.text: Different mean and, especially, different **standard deviation**

items: The **normal distribution domain** was chosen for its mathematical **flexibility and tractability**.
z scores (for example the Cardio Z app) span sizes **from fetus to adults** and imaging modalities **from echocardiography to MRI**.
z values make echo vs autopsy differences **less important**.

explanation.text: The limitation of standardization is that what is normal, and the scatter in the measurements of normal, vary from population to population. This is particularly true of the standard deviation, which forms the denominator of the z score equation.

choiceNotes.b: z scores are available for sizes from **fetus to adults** (Cardio Z).
choiceNotes.c: z scores incorporate imaging modalities from echocardiography to **MRI**.
choiceNotes.d: The opposite: differences between echo and autopsy measurements become **less important** when z values are used.
choiceNotes.e: The normal distribution domain was chosen **because of** its mathematical flexibility and tractability.

stem: Autopsy specimens are a main source of normal valve dimensions used in surgical decisions. Dimensions are similar in fresh and fixed specimens, with one exception. Which exception does the source describe?

choices.text: Semilunar valves are smaller after any fixation
Tricuspid valve and right heart are larger with pressure fixation
The mitral valve is about 33% larger with pressure fixation
All valves are about 20% larger in fresh specimens
Left heart dimensions are larger with pressure fixation

explanation.text: Fresh and fixed specimens give similar dimensions, **except** that with **pressure fixation** the **tricuspid valve and right heart** dimensions are somewhat larger.

items: Postmortem and in vivo measurements may not be exact, but they are **generally similar**.
Dimensions in autopsy specimens from **normal children** are similar to those obtained by **imaging**.
So autopsy and imaging data are both attractive for **clinical decisions**.

explanation.title: Don't mix the percentages
explanation.text: "About 33%" and "about 20%" larger describe **echocardiographic vs autopsy** mitral valve dimensions, not fresh vs fixed specimens.

Scholz and colleagues found that dimensions are similar in both fresh and fixed specimens (except that when pressure fixation is used, the tricuspid valve and right heart dimensions are somewhat larger)

choiceNotes.a: The exception concerns the **tricuspid valve and right heart** with pressure fixation, not the semilunar valves.
choiceNotes.c: About 33% larger is the difference of **echocardiographic** mitral dimensions vs autopsy in subjects below about 0.5 m² BSA.
choiceNotes.d: About 20% larger is the difference of **echocardiographic** (Riggs) vs autopsy mitral dimensions above 1 m² BSA, not fresh vs fixed specimens.
choiceNotes.e: With pressure fixation it is the **right** heart (and tricuspid valve) that is somewhat larger, not the left heart.

source.loc: p. 25, Use of Standardized Cardiac Dimensions in Surgical Decisions

stem: An infant's mitral valve diameter by echocardiography is compared with autopsy-based normal values, and the two measurement methods are known to differ. How does the source say such differences between methods are best made **less important**?

choices.text: Use only autopsy data and disregard echocardiography
Express the diameter in centimeters without normalization
Wait until modality-specific normal values are published
Express the dimension as a z value relative to normal
Divide the diameter by the descending aortic diameter

explanation.text: Differences between echocardiographic and autopsy measurements **become less important when z values are used** to indicate differences from normal.
Normal values are generally not available in each modality, so dimensions must be related to available normal values, even if from a different modality. z values reduce the impact of the mismatch.
Any differences between echocardiographic and autopsy measurements become less important when z values are used to indicate differences from normal.

choiceNotes.a: Both sources are attractive for clinical decisions because of the extensive data available.
choiceNotes.b: Plain centimeters are unacceptable when patients range from very young to very old.
choiceNotes.c: Normal values are generally not available in each modality; dimensions are related to available values, even from a different modality.
choiceNotes.e: That is a **ratio** to another structure; it does not address echo vs autopsy differences.

source.loc: p. 25, Use of Standardized Cardiac Dimensions in Surgical Decisions
p. 24, Dimensions of the Pathway; Normalization of Pathway Dimensions

stem: The chapter's autopsy reference table of normal children (Table 1.1) lists the diameters of all four cardiac valves by body surface area. At any given BSA in this table, which order, from **largest to smallest**, is shown?

choices.text: Mitral > tricuspid > aortic > pulmonary
Pulmonary > aortic > tricuspid > mitral
Tricuspid > mitral > pulmonary > aortic
Tricuspid > pulmonary > mitral > aortic
Mitral > tricuspid > pulmonary > aortic

explanation.text: In Table 1.1, at every BSA: **tricuspid > mitral > pulmonary > aortic**.

items: **Table 1.1**: autopsy hearts of apparently normal children (oldest 15 years); mean ± SD by BSA for all four valves.
**Table 1.2**: aortic and pulmonary valve diameters by BSA range **and sex**; the pulmonary valve is larger than the aortic in every row.
**Table 1.3**: echocardiographic mitral (minor A-P and major lateral axes) and tricuspid diameters in normal children.

explanation.text: Use these tables as **guides to normal size by BSA**; compare a patient's valve with the mean and SD for the same BSA (that is, as a z value).
Useful guides to normal sizes of AV and semilunar valves by BSA (m^2^) and sex are available from autopsy studies (Tables 1.1 and 1.2).

choiceNotes.a: In Table 1.1 the tricuspid is larger than the mitral, and the pulmonary larger than the aortic.
choiceNotes.b: The atrioventricular valves (tricuspid, mitral) are larger than the semilunar valves at every BSA.
choiceNotes.d: The mitral valve is larger than the pulmonary valve at every BSA (for example 20.1 vs 15.3 mm at 1.0 m²).
choiceNotes.e: The tricuspid valve, not the mitral, is the largest at every BSA.

source.loc: p. 25, Use of Standardized Cardiac Dimensions in Surgical Decisions; Table 1.1
